concepts.title: List, Set, and Map: Choosing the Right Collection
concepts.description: List, Set, and Map are the three foundational collection interfaces in java.util. Each has its own contract (ordered and index-accessible, duplicate-free, or key-to-value lookup), and choosing ArrayList vs LinkedList, or HashSet vs a sorted alternative, comes down to which operations need to be fast.
learningObjectives: Explain the core contract each of List, Set, and Map guarantees, and choose the right one for a given data shape.
Explain the practical performance difference between ArrayList and LinkedList for common operations (indexed access, adding/removing at the end vs. in the middle).
Explain what makes an object usable as a HashSet element or HashMap key, in terms of equals() and hashCode() being consistent with each other.
Predict and explain a bug caused by using a mutable object as a HashMap key or HashSet element and then mutating it after insertion.
Use the core methods of List, Set, and Map (add/remove/get/contains, put/get/containsKey, iteration) correctly.
Explain why List and Set are declared as interface types on the left of a declaration (List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();) rather than the concrete implementation type.

sections.heading: Three Contracts, Three Shapes of Data
List Implementations: ArrayList vs LinkedList
sections.body:
`ArrayList` stores its elements in a resizable internal array, so indexed access (`list.get(i)`) takes the same time regardless of the list's size: it is an array lookup at a computed offset. Adding at the *end* is normally just as cheap, except on the occasions when the internal array is full and has to be reallocated to a larger one (an amortized cost you don't need to think about on each call). The cost shows up for insertion or removal in the *middle* or at the *front*: every element after that point has to be shifted over by one slot to make room (or close the gap), which takes time proportional to the number of elements after the insertion point.

`LinkedList` stores elements as a chain of nodes, each holding a value and links to the next and previous node. Adding or removing at the very front or back takes constant time regardless of size, because only the first or last node's links change and nothing is shifted. But `list.get(i)` has to walk the chain from one end, node by node, until it reaches position `i`. On a large list that is much slower than the same call on an `ArrayList`, especially inside a loop that calls `get(i)` for every `i`, which turns a linear scan into a quadratic one.

The rule of thumb: default to `ArrayList` unless you need frequent insertion or removal at the front, or you are building a queue or deque where a node-based structure fits better. Code that just accumulates elements and reads them back never needs LinkedList's strengths, and for a plain queue `ArrayDeque` is usually the better choice anyway.

sections.heading: Set and Map: equals() and hashCode() Have to Agree
The Mutable-Key Trap: Don't Change What You've Already Hashed

examples.title: List Permits Duplicates, Set Silently Rejects Them
examples.explanation: visits is a List, so it records every add() call in order, including the second "home". A List says nothing about uniqueness, so all three entries exist and size() reports 3. new HashSet<>(visits) builds a Set from those elements, and the no-duplicates contract collapses the two "home" entries into one, so uniquePages has size 2. Wrapping a list in a HashSet (or a LinkedHashSet, if the original order matters) is a common way to deduplicate it or to count distinct values without writing duplicate-checking logic yourself.

examples.title: HashMap Needs equals() and hashCode() to Find a Key
examples.explanation: The Product passed to get(...) is a brand-new object, constructed separately from the one originally put into the map. It is not the same object in memory. Yet inventory.get(...) correctly finds and returns 5, because HashMap's lookup relies on hashCode() to locate the right bucket and equals() to confirm the match once there, and Product overrides both consistently based on sku. Had Product relied on Object's default, identity-based equals() and hashCode() (by not overriding them), this lookup would return null: the two Product objects, despite representing the same SKU, would be considered unrelated, since their default hash codes and default equals() checks are based on their distinct memory identities, not their content.

examples.title: The Mutable-Key Bug in Action
examples.explanation: Once key.add("b") runs, the List's hashCode() (which depends on its current contents) changes. The HashMap placed the entry using the hash code key had at insertion and has no way to learn that it changed. The map still holds the entry, but containsKey(key) computes the new hash code, looks in the bucket that points to, and finds nothing, because the entry is still in the bucket the old hash code selected. That is why mutable types like ArrayList make risky HashMap keys: nothing throws, and the entry you definitely put in seems to have vanished. (For some mutations the new hash happens to land in the same bucket and the lookup still fails, because the stored hash no longer matches, so a stale key is never safe.)

misconceptions.description: A Set automatically keeps its elements sorted or in insertion order, since it's meant to represent a clean, well-organized collection of unique items.
misconceptions.clarification: Uniqueness and ordering are separate guarantees, and plain Set (and its most common implementation, HashSet) only promises the first one. HashSet's iteration order is unspecified and depends on hash bucket placement, so it can look arbitrary and can change between Java versions or after the set grows. If you need insertion order, use LinkedHashSet; if you need sorted order, use TreeSet. Assuming HashSet keeps any order is a common reason output "looks wrong" even though every element is present.
misconceptions.fact: Uniqueness and ordering are two completely separate guarantees, and plain Set (and its most common implementation, HashSet) only promises the first one.

misconceptions.description: Overriding equals() on a class is sufficient on its own to make that class work correctly as a HashSet element or HashMap key.
misconceptions.clarification: equals() and hashCode() have to be overridden together, or hash-based collections break in a subtle way. Objects that are .equals() to each other MUST return the same hashCode(). If only equals() is overridden and hashCode() keeps its identity-based default, two .equals() objects can have different hash codes, so a HashSet or HashMap searches the wrong bucket and contains() or get() returns false or null for an object that .equals() says is present. This is not a missed optimization. It violates a contract that hash-based collections rely on to work at all.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: numbers is a List. Does its contract remove or reject the duplicate 20 when it is constructed?
unique is built by passing numbers into a HashSet constructor. What does a Set's no-duplicates contract do to the repeated value during that construction?
Trace the loop that builds countByValue for each of the four numbers. getOrDefault(n, 0) + 1 increments a running count per distinct value.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 4, then 3, then 2. numbers keeps all four elements, including the duplicate 20, because Lists allow duplicates. unique collapses the two 20s into one, leaving 3 distinct values. countByValue counts occurrences per value, and 20 appears twice, so its count is 2.
exercises.solutionExplanation: numbers.size() is 4 because a List never removes duplicates, so all four values passed to List.of(...) are present. unique.size() is 3 because constructing a HashSet applies the no-duplicates guarantee and collapses the two 20 entries, leaving 10, 20, and 30. countByValue.get(20) is 2 because the loop increments a running count per value, with getOrDefault(n, 0) starting a value's count at 0 the first time it is seen. Since 20 appears twice in numbers, its count is incremented twice.

exercises.prompt: This class is meant to let two Coordinate objects representing the same (x, y) position be treated as equal, and be usable correctly as keys in a HashMap. It compiles fine, but the assertion below fails. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Coordinate overrides equals() to compare x and y. Does it override hashCode() to match?
Without a matching hashCode() override, Coordinate inherits Object's identity-based hashCode(), which ignores x and y.
Add a hashCode() override, typically using Objects.hash(x, y), so two Coordinates with the same x and y always produce the same hash code.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Coordinate overrides equals() to compare x and y, but never overrides hashCode(), so it inherits Object's identity-based version. Two Coordinates with identical x and y but different identities produce different hash codes. containsKey() first computes the hash code of the lookup key to choose a bucket, and only then calls equals() on the candidates in that bucket. If new Coordinate(1, 1) hashes to a different bucket than the stored entry, equals() never runs and containsKey() returns false even though the two objects are .equals(). Adding a hashCode() based on the same fields equals() uses (via Objects.hash(x, y)) guarantees that .equals() objects hash identically, so HashMap finds the right bucket and then confirms the match.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes when ArrayList is likely to be noticeably slower than LinkedList for the same sequence of operations?
options: Reading elements by index (get(i)) in a large loop -- ArrayList's array-based storage makes indexed access slow.
Inserting or removing an element near the FRONT of a large list repeatedly.
Iterating over every element in order with a for-each loop -- ArrayList is fundamentally incapable of sequential iteration.
Adding elements to the END of the list one at a time -- ArrayList cannot do this efficiently at all.
assessments.explanation: Repeated insertion or removal near the front of an ArrayList forces every subsequent element to be physically shifted by one slot on each such operation, which costs time proportional to the list's size every single time. LinkedList avoids this for front operations, since it only ever has to relink a couple of node pointers, regardless of how many elements exist elsewhere in the list. The “Reading elements by index (get(i))…” option is backwards: indexed get(i) is ArrayList's strength (a direct array-offset lookup) and LinkedList's weakness (it has to walk the chain). The “Adding elements to the END…” option is false: appending to the end of an ArrayList is normally an instant, amortized-constant-time operation. The “Iterating over every element in order…” option is false: ArrayList iterates perfectly well in order; there's no fundamental incapacity there at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a class that overrides equals() to compare objects by their content, but doesn't also override hashCode(), can cause a HashSet or HashMap to behave incorrectly -- specifically, why a lookup can fail to find an object that is genuinely already present according to equals().
assessments.modelAnswer: HashSet and HashMap rely on hashing for fast operations: when an object is inserted, its hashCode() is computed and used to decide which internal storage bucket it goes into; when a lookup happens later, the hash code of the object being looked up is computed the same way, to figure out which single bucket needs to be searched, and only within that one bucket does equals() get used to check for a match against whatever else is already there. For this two-step process to work, there's a strict contract every class has to honor: any two objects that are .equals() to each other must produce the same hashCode(). If a class overrides equals() to compare by content but leaves hashCode() as Object's default, which is based on the object's identity, essentially its memory address, then two separately-constructed objects holding identical data will be .equals() to each other (since the content matches) but will very likely compute different hash codes (since they're different objects in memory). The practical consequence shows up at lookup time: inserting one such object stores it in whichever bucket its hash code points to; looking it up later via a different-but-equal object computes a different hash code and searches a different bucket, where the original entry was never placed. Because the search never even reaches the bucket containing the match, equals() never gets a chance to run and confirm anything. The lookup reports 'not found' even though an equals()-equal object is sitting in the collection, just in the wrong bucket as far as this particular lookup's hash code is concerned. The fix is always to override hashCode() alongside equals(), deriving both from the exact same set of fields, so that equal objects are guaranteed to compute equal hash codes and therefore always land in, and get searched in, the same bucket.

assessments.prompt: Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>(); boolean firstAdd = tags.add("java"); boolean secondAdd = tags.add("java"); System.out.println(firstAdd + " " + secondAdd); What prints?
options: true false, because add() returns whether the element was actually newly added -- the first call adds "java" and returns true, the second call finds it already present, does nothing, and returns false.
false true, because add() reports whether the set's size changed as a result of the call, and duplicate detection happens only after size is already checked.
This throws an exception on the second add() call, because Set forbids adding a value that's already a duplicate.
true true, because add() always returns true whenever it's given a valid, non-null argument.
assessments.explanation: A Set's core contract guarantees no duplicates, and add() communicates whether it changed anything by returning a boolean: true if the element was new and got added, false if an equal element was already present and the call was a no-op. The first add("java") has nothing to collide with yet, so it succeeds and returns true; the second finds "java" already there, changes nothing, and returns false. The “true true, because add() always returns true…” option is wrong because add() reports success or no-op, not a constant true. The “This throws an exception on the second…” option is wrong because attempting to add a duplicate is not an error condition in Java: it's an ordinary, silent no-op. The “false true, because add() reports whether…” option garbles the mechanism; there's no separate 'size check before duplicate check' step.

assessments.prompt: List<Integer> key = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)); Map<List<Integer>, String> map = new HashMap<>(); map.put(key, "first"); key.add(2); System.out.println(map.get(key)); What is the most likely outcome, and why?
options: "first" -- HashMap always finds a key by checking every stored entry one by one with equals(), so mutating the key afterward doesn't matter.
"first" -- HashMap automatically detects the mutation and re-hashes every affected key entry on the spot.
This throws a ConcurrentModificationException, since a list that's currently a live map key can never be mutated.
Often null -- mutating key after insertion changes its hashCode() (since List's hash code depends on its current contents).
assessments.explanation: HashMap locates entries by computing a key's hash code to pick a bucket, and List's hashCode() is defined in terms of its current elements, so key.add(2) changes what key.hashCode() returns. The entry itself is still physically sitting in the bucket the original hash code pointed to, but map.get(key) computes key's new, current hash code and looks in a different bucket, one that was never given this entry. Nothing throws; the lookup fails silently. The “"first" -- HashMap always finds a key…” option misdescribes HashMap's lookup mechanism, which is bucket-based, not a scan of every entry. The “This throws a ConcurrentModificationException, since a list…” option invents a protection Java's mutable collections don't have. The “"first" -- HashMap automatically detects the mutation…” option describes a re-hashing-on-mutation feature that HashMap does not implement: it has no way to even detect that a key it's holding was just mutated elsewhere.

assessments.prompt: Why is List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); generally preferred over ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); for a local variable only ever used through basic List operations?
options: There's no real difference at all; it's purely a stylistic preference with no practical consequence either way.
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); runs measurably faster at run time, since interface-typed method calls skip virtual dispatch entirely.

Declaring the variable's type as the interface means every use of names is checked only against List's contract, so the concrete implementation on the right-hand side can later be swapped (to LinkedList, say) by changing just that one line, without touching any other code that only ever called List methods on names.
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); actually fails to compile, since a variable's declared type is required to be an interface whenever a generic collection is involved.
assessments.explanation: Declaring the left-hand type as the interface restricts what the rest of the code is allowed to assume about names: only List's own contract, nothing ArrayList-specific. That's what makes swapping the implementation later a one-line change: as long as every other use of names only ever called List methods, changing just the right-hand side to new LinkedList<>() keeps everything else compiling and working unchanged. The “There's no real difference at all; it's…” option understates a, practical software-engineering benefit. The “ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); actually fails…” option is false: declaring a variable with a class type is completely legal Java. The “List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); runs measurably…” option is fabricated; there is no such blanket run-time performance difference from the declared type of a reference variable.

concepts.title: Generics and Type Erasure
concepts.description: Generics let a class or method be parameterized by a type, catching type mismatches at compile time instead of at a runtime ClassCastException, but the compiler achieves this by erasing all that type information after compilation, and understanding what type erasure removes (and what it doesn't) explains several otherwise-baffling generics restrictions and warnings.
learningObjectives: Explain what problem generics solve, contrasted with a pre-generics collection of Object with manual casting.
Declare and use a generic class and a generic method with a type parameter, and explain what a bounded type parameter (<T extends Comparable<T>>) adds.
Explain type erasure: what the compiler does with type parameter information after compile time, and why List<String> and List<Integer> share exactly one Class object at run time.
Predict and explain why you cannot create a generic array (new T[10]) directly, and why instanceof cannot check against a parameterized type.
Explain wildcard basics (? extends T vs ? super T) at a conceptual level -- reading from a producer vs writing to a consumer.
Predict the exact unchecked-cast or compile-time behavior of a small generics code snippet involving erasure.

sections.heading: The Problem Generics Solve: Casting Everywhere, Caught Too Late
sections.body:
Before generics (Java 5), a general-purpose container like `List` could only hold `Object` references, and there was no way to tell the compiler that a list only holds `String`s. Reading an element back out required a cast, which was a promise the programmer made to the compiler with nothing checking it:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();      // pre-generics style -- holds raw Objects
names.add("Amy");
names.add(42);                       // compiles fine -- nothing stops a wrong type from going in

String first = (String) names.get(0);   // fine
String second = (String) names.get(1);  // compiles fine, throws ClassCastException at RUN TIME
```

The bug, an `Integer` going into a list that was meant to hold `String`s, is invisible where it happens (`names.add(42);` compiles because `names` holds any `Object`). It only surfaces later, at the cast, possibly in a different part of the program, as a `ClassCastException`. Generics close the gap by letting you state the element type up front: with `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`, `names.add(42);` is a compile-time error, because `42` (an `int`, autoboxed to `Integer`) isn't a `String`. The mistake is caught on the line where it is made.

sections.heading: Generic Classes and Methods: Parameterizing Over a Type
Type Erasure: Generics Are a Compile-Time Illusion
sections.body:
Here is the detail that explains almost every 'weird' generics restriction you'll run into: Java implements generics through **type erasure**. The compiler uses your type parameters (`<T>`, `<String>`, whatever) to check your code for type correctness *at compile time*, and then, when producing the bytecode, it **erases** that information: a type parameter with no bound is replaced with `Object` everywhere it's used, and all the casts needed to make that safe are inserted automatically by the compiler. At run time, there is no `T` anywhere in the compiled `.class` file at all.

The most checkable consequence: `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are backed by the exact same `.class` file (well, its implementation, like `ArrayList.class`), and produce the exact same `Class` object at run time:

```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> integers = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(strings.getClass() == integers.getClass());   // true!
```

This is surprising the first time you see it. It looks like these should be two different types, since the compiler treats them so differently, but by the time the JVM is running the program, both variables' run-time class is just `ArrayList`, full stop; the `<String>` and `<Integer>` information existed purely for the compiler's own type-checking and was thrown away afterward. This is also why `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` cannot be used as two separate overloads (`void process(List<String> l)` and `void process(List<Integer> l)` in the same class is a compile error, 'name clash'): after erasure, both methods would have the exact same erased signature, `process(List)`, and Java cannot have two methods with identical signatures.

sections.heading: What Erasure Forbids: Generic Arrays and instanceof Against a Parameterized Type
Wildcards: ? extends T (Producer) and ? super T (Consumer)
sections.body:
Wildcards let a method accept a *range* of related parameterized types rather than one exact one. `List<? extends Number>` means 'a `List` of some unknown specific type that is `Number` or a subtype of it', you can safely *read* elements out of it (each one is guaranteed to be at least a `Number`), but you cannot safely *add* to it (the list's element type might be `Integer`, and adding a plain `Double` would violate that, so the compiler forbids adding anything except `null`, to stay safe). `List<? super Integer>` means 'a `List` of some unknown type that is `Integer` or a supertype of it', you can safely *add* `Integer`s to it (any such list is guaranteed to be able to hold an `Integer`), but reading from it only gives you back `Object` (the compiler can't promise anything more specific than that about what's stored).

The common mnemonic is **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super**: if your method is treating the parameterized collection as a source of values it reads (a 'producer'), use `? extends T`; if it's treating the collection as a destination it writes into (a 'consumer'), use `? super T`. A method like `double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers)` only ever reads from `numbers` to add up a total, so `? extends Number` is right: it lets callers pass a `List<Integer>`, a `List<Double>`, or a `List<Number>` itself, all of which the plain, unbounded `List<Number>` parameter type would have rejected.

examples.title: Erasure Means List<String> and List<Integer> Are the Same Class at Run Time
examples.explanation: getClass() reports the run-time class, and for both lists it is ArrayList, with no trace of String or Integer. The <String> and <Integer> in the source are compile-time information: javac uses them to check that only Strings go into strings and only Integers into integers, and to spare you casts when reading elements back. That checking is finished when compilation ends, and the bytecode does not distinguish the two lists. This is what erasure means: the type parameter is removed from the compiled code, leaving the raw type or its bound (here Object, since List<T> has no bound).

examples.title: A Bounded Type Parameter Enables a Generic Max-Finder
examples.explanation: <T extends Comparable<T>> tells the compiler that whatever T ends up being, it must implement Comparable<T>, which is what makes item.compareTo(largest) legal inside the method body; without that bound, T could be any type at all, including ones with no compareTo() method whatsoever, and the method wouldn't compile. Integer and String both implement Comparable<Integer> and Comparable<String> respectively (as part of the standard library), so max() works correctly for both List<Integer> and List<String>: one single method definition, type-checked once, reused for every type that satisfies the bound. Passing a List of some type that does NOT implement Comparable would fail at the call site itself, at compile time, with a clear type-bound violation, not as a runtime surprise deep inside the loop.

examples.title: PECS in Practice: A Producer Parameter and a Consumer Parameter
examples.explanation: sum() only ever reads elements out of numbers (via the for-each loop) to accumulate a total, so it's a producer of values from the caller's point of view, ? extends Number lets it accept a List<Integer>, a List<Double>, or a List<Number> itself, any of which is guaranteed to hand back something that's at least a Number when read. A plain List<Number> parameter would have rejected List<Integer>, since List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number> in Java's type system, despite Integer being a subtype of Number. fillWithSquares() only ever writes into destination, so it's a consumer, ? super Integer lets it accept a List<Number> or List<Object>, either of which is guaranteed to be able to hold an Integer safely, without needing destination to be List<Integer>. Trying to read a specific type back out of a ? super Integer parameter would only ever give you Object, which is why consumer-style wildcards are for writing, not reading.

misconceptions.description: Because List<String> and List<Integer> are clearly different, incompatible types at compile time, they must also be different classes at run time, each with their own distinct Class object.
misconceptions.clarification: This is backwards from how type erasure works. The compiler enforces the distinction between List<String> and List<Integer> during compilation (checking every add() and assignment against the declared type parameter) and then discards that type parameter information when producing bytecode. At run time, both are represented by the exact same class (typically ArrayList, or whatever implementation was used), and calling .getClass() on either returns the identical Class object. The type safety generics provide is a compile-time guarantee about how your source code is allowed to use a collection, not a run-time property the JVM can inspect or distinguish between afterward.

misconceptions.description: You should be able to write if (someList instanceof List<String>) to check, at run time, whether a list specifically holds Strings.
misconceptions.clarification: This specific check is a compile-time error in Java, not merely bad practice: because of type erasure, there is no run-time representation of the parameterized type List<String> distinct from plain List for the JVM to check against; the <String> part doesn't exist anymore once compilation is finished. The compiler only permits the unparameterized check, someList instanceof List, which tells you it's a List of *something*, with no way to ask what that something is via instanceof. If you need to verify element types at run time, that requires manually inspecting individual elements (e.g., checking each element with instanceof String) rather than trying to check the collection's declared type parameter, which was never preserved past compile time.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Both namesPair and numbersPair are instances of the same generic class Pair, with different type arguments. After type erasure, does .getClass() see any difference between Pair<String> and Pair<Integer>?
getClass() reports the run-time class, which does not depend on the type argument used to construct the Pair.
namesPair.getFirst() returns a T that the compiler knows, from namesPair's declared type, is a String, so no cast is needed to call a String method on it.
exercises.expectedAnswer: true, then AMY. namesPair and numbersPair are both instances of the same erased class Pair, so their getClass() results are identical despite the different type arguments. namesPair.getFirst() returns "Amy", and .toUpperCase() gives "AMY".
exercises.solutionExplanation: Pair<String> and Pair<Integer> are both, after erasure, instances of the one class Pair: the type argument used at construction time (String or Integer) has no bearing on the object's run-time class, so namesPair.getClass() == numbersPair.getClass() is true, analogous to List<String> and List<Integer> sharing ArrayList.class. Separately, namesPair.getFirst() returns the value stored in first for that specific instance, "Amy", and because namesPair was declared as Pair<String>, the compiler already knows getFirst()'s return type is String for this call, inserting whatever cast is needed automatically, so calling .toUpperCase() on the result compiles and runs without any cast being written, producing "AMY".

exercises.prompt: This generic Stack class is meant to store items in a plain array internally, but it fails to compile. Find and fix the bug, explaining why the original line is illegal.
hints: Creating an array requires the JVM to know the element type at run time. Does T still exist as a type at run time, after type erasure?
The standard workaround is to back the generic class with an Object array internally instead of a T array.
You will need a cast back to T (which the compiler flags as unchecked) when reading an element out of the Object array in pop().
exercises.solutionExplanation: new T[capacity] is illegal because, after type erasure, T no longer exists as a type at the point the array would be created: the JVM needs an element type to allocate an array (arrays track their element type at run time for array-store checks), and there's nothing left for T to be at that point. The standard, idiomatic workaround, used internally by generic collection classes like ArrayList, is to back the class with a plain Object[] instead, which is always legal to create. push() stores items into that Object[] without needing any cast (every T is already an Object). pop(), however, needs to hand back a T to its caller, and reading an Object out of items and treating it as a T requires a cast, (T) items[--size], one the compiler cannot fully verify is safe at run time (since T is erased), which is why it's paired with @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") to acknowledge that the class's own internal logic (only ever storing T values via push()) is what guarantees the cast's safety, not anything the compiler itself can check.

assessments.prompt: Why does Java forbid writing if (someList instanceof List<String>)?
options: Because instanceof only works on final classes, and List is an interface.
Because instanceof can never be used with any interface type, generic or not.
Because List<String> is not actually a subtype of List at run time.
Because after type erasure, there is no run-time representation of List<String> distinct from plain List -- the JVM has nothing to check the parameterized type against.
assessments.explanation: Type erasure removes type parameter information from the bytecode: at run time an ArrayList of Strings and an ArrayList of Integers are the same class, with nothing marking one as 'holds Strings'. instanceof asks a run-time question, and List<String> does not exist as a distinct run-time type after erasure, so the compiler rejects the check instead of letting it mean less than it appears to. The “Because instanceof can never be used…” option is false: instanceof works fine with interfaces generally (unparameterized ones, like plain List, are checked constantly). The “Because List<String> is not actually a subtype…” option is a nonsensical claim about subtyping, not the reason. The “Because instanceof only works on final classes…” option is fabricated: instanceof has no such final-class restriction.

assessments.prompt: Explain type erasure to a developer who is confused about why they can't create a generic array (new T[10]) inside a generic class, even though the class compiles fine everywhere else it uses T.
assessments.modelAnswer: Java implements generics using type erasure: the compiler uses your type parameters, like T in a generic class, to check that your code uses types consistently while you're writing and compiling it, but once compilation finishes, that type parameter information is discarded from the resulting bytecode. Wherever an unbounded T appeared in your source, the compiled class effectively treats it as Object, inserting whatever casts are needed automatically so the erased code still behaves correctly. This is why, for instance, List<String> and List<Integer> end up being represented by the exact same run-time class: there's no T, no String, no Integer baked into the compiled class file at all; that information only ever existed for the compiler's own benefit, during the one phase where it's checking your code. The reason this breaks new T[10] is that creating an array in Java is not just about type-checking: arrays must know their own element type at run time, so that the JVM can perform array-store checks (rejecting, say, an attempt to put a String into an Integer[] at run time). By the time new T[10] would execute, T has already been erased and no longer corresponds to any type the JVM could give the new array as its element type. There's nothing left to create an array of. This is why generic classes that need an internal array, like the standard library's own ArrayList, are implemented by creating a plain Object[] internally instead, and inserting a (marked-unchecked) cast back to T whenever an element needs to be handed back out to a caller as that specific type, a workaround that only exists because of, and only makes sense once you understand, type erasure.

assessments.prompt: List names = new ArrayList(); names.add("Amy"); names.add(42); String first = (String) names.get(0); String second = (String) names.get(1); Which line is the actual root cause of the bug here, and when does the problem actually surface?
options: names.add(42); is the root cause -- a value of the wrong intended type entering the raw, unparameterized list -- but with no type parameter for the compiler to check against, this line compiles without complaint; the problem only surfaces later, as a ClassCastException at the cast on a following line, in a different part of the code from where the actual mistake was made.
String second = (String) names.get(1); is the root cause, since casts are inherently unsafe and should never appear in correct code.
There is no actual bug here; this code compiles and runs correctly, printing normally.
names.add(42); is the root cause, and the compiler catches it immediately at that exact line, before the program can even run.
assessments.explanation: names is declared as a raw List, with no element type parameter for the compiler to enforce, so names.add(42) compiles just as readily as names.add("Amy") did, since both are legal Objects as far as an unparameterized List is concerned. The mistake (putting an Integer into a list only ever meant to hold Strings) is invisible right where it happens. It only becomes visible much later, when (String) names.get(1) tries to cast that Integer to String and the JVM throws ClassCastException at run time, in code that may be far removed from the add() call that caused the problem. The “names.add(42); is the root cause, and the compiler…” option wrongly assumes the compiler tracks intended element types on a raw list. The “String second = (String) names.get(1)…” option blames the cast itself rather than the type mismatch the cast merely exposes. The “There is no actual bug here…” option is wrong because this exact sequence is the runtime-ClassCastException bug generics were introduced to catch earlier.

assessments.prompt: public static <T> T max(List<T> items) { T largest = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.compareTo(largest) > 0) { largest = item; } } return largest; } Why does this specific method fail to compile as written?
options: for-each loops can never be used with a type parameter that has no explicit bound, under any circumstance.

T has no bound here, so the compiler only knows T is some type extending Object -- and Object declares no compareTo() method, so item.compareTo(largest) doesn't resolve to any method the compiler can find; T needs to be declared as <T extends Comparable<T>> for that call to be legal.
It compiles fine exactly as written, for any type T supplied at the call site.
List<T> is illegal syntax on a method parameter; it must be written as List<? extends T> instead.
assessments.explanation: With no bound on T, all the compiler can assume about it is that it's some subtype of Object, and Object has no compareTo() method at all, so item.compareTo(largest) fails to compile, since there's no guarantee whatever type T ends up being supports that call. Adding a bound, <T extends Comparable<T>>, restricts T to only types that do implement Comparable<T>, which is what makes compareTo() a legal call inside the method body. The “It compiles fine exactly as written…” option ignores this missing bound. The “for-each loops can never be used…” option is fabricated: for-each loops work fine over List<T> regardless of any bound on T; the failure is about calling compareTo(), not about iterating. The “List<T> is illegal syntax on a method…” option is wrong: List<T> as an ordinary parameter type is completely standard generic syntax.

assessments.prompt: A method needs to copy every element out of a source list into a destination list, only ever reading from source and only ever writing into destination, without requiring either list to be an exact type match for T. Following PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super), which parameter types are correct for static <T> void copy(source, destination)?
options: List<? extends T> source, List<? extends T> destination -- both parameters should use extends, since both are Lists related to T.
List<? super T> source, List<? extends T> destination -- source produces values, so it should use super, and destination consumes them, so it should use extends.
List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination -- source is only ever read from (a producer of values), so it uses extends.
List<T> source, List<T> destination -- wildcards are never appropriate when copying between two lists that share the same type parameter T.
assessments.explanation: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. source is only read from inside copy(), producing the values being moved, so ? extends T is correct, letting callers pass a List<Integer> or any other subtype-of-T list as the source. destination is only written into, consuming those values, so ? super T is correct, letting callers pass a List<Number> or any other supertype-of-T list as the destination, as long as it's guaranteed able to hold a T. The “List<? super T> source, List<? extends T>…” option reverses the two roles. The “List<T> source, List<T> destination -- wildcards…” option would work but is needlessly restrictive, forcing both lists to be List<T> when callers might reasonably want to pass related, non-identical types. The “List<? extends T> source, List<? extends T>…” option would let source work correctly but would break destination, since adding a T to a List<? extends T> is the operation Java's wildcard rules forbid, for safety.

concepts.title: Comparable vs. Comparator
concepts.description: Comparable defines a class's own single, natural ordering via compareTo(), baked into the class itself, while Comparator defines an ordering from the outside, letting the same objects be sorted in as many different ways as you need, without ever touching the class being sorted.
learningObjectives: Implement Comparable<T> on a class to define its natural ordering, and explain what compareTo()'s return value's sign (negative/zero/positive) actually means.
Write a Comparator<T> as a separate object to sort the same class in a different, non-natural order, using both a class and a lambda.
Use Comparator's chaining methods (thenComparing, reversed) to build a multi-key sort without writing a manual multi-condition compareTo.
Explain why a class can have only one natural ordering (one compareTo()) but arbitrarily many Comparators.
Predict the outcome of Collections.sort()/List.sort() given a specific Comparable implementation or Comparator, including sorting in descending order.
Identify and fix a broken compareTo() implementation that violates the required sign contract, such as through unsafe subtraction.

sections.heading: Comparable<T>: A Class's Own, Single Natural Ordering
Comparator<T>: Ordering Defined From the Outside, as Many Ways as You Need
sections.body:
A class can implement `Comparable` only once, so it has one natural order. But programs often need to sort the same objects in different ways: employees by salary in one report, by name in another. A `Comparator<T>` is a separate object, not a method on the class being sorted, that defines one ordering, and you can write as many for a type as you need.

```java
Comparator<Employee> byNameLambda = (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName());

employees.sort(byNameLambda);
System.out.println(employees);   // sorted by name, completely independent of Employee's own compareTo()
```

`Employee` needs no changes for this: `byNameLambda` lives outside the class, and `List.sort(Comparator<T>)` uses it instead of the elements' `compareTo()`. That is the difference. `Comparable` is something the class author builds in once, for the one ordering the class considers natural. A `Comparator` can be defined by any caller, from outside, and unrelated pieces of code can each define their own `Comparator<Employee>` without coordinating or touching `Employee`.

sections.heading: Chaining Comparators: thenComparing and reversed, Instead of a Manual Multi-Key compareTo
sections.body:
Sorting by more than one key ('by grade, then by GPA within each grade') used to mean writing a manual `compareTo`-style method with an if/else cascade checking each key in turn. `Comparator`'s default methods (`thenComparing`, `reversed`, and the static factory method `comparing`) build this compositionally, without any manual cascade at all:

```java
Comparator<Student> byGradeThenGpaDesc = Comparator
        .comparing((Student s) -> s.grade)
        .thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder());

students.sort(byGradeThenGpaDesc);
```

`Comparator.comparing(s -> s.grade)` builds a `Comparator` that compares two `Student`s by whatever `grade` holds (relying on that field's own natural ordering: `String`'s, here); `.thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder())` chains a second key that's only consulted to break ties when the first comparison result is zero (same grade), and orders that tie-break by descending GPA. `.reversed()` on any `Comparator` produces a new one with the ordering flipped, without needing a separate, hand-written 'descending' version of the same comparison logic. This compositional style avoids an entire class of bugs that hand-written multi-condition `compareTo`/`compare` methods are prone to: forgetting to handle the tie-break case correctly, or getting the sign backwards in one branch of a large if/else chain.

sections.heading: A Broken compareTo(): Contract Violations That Corrupt Sorting Silently

examples.title: Comparable Gives a Class Its Natural Order
examples.explanation: Collections.sort(tasks) needs no second argument specifying how to compare Tasks, because Task itself declares its natural order via compareTo(), which compares by priority ascending using Integer.compare, a safe alternative to this.priority - other.priority that avoids any risk of overflow for extreme int values. The sort correctly orders tasks from lowest priority number (1, 'Fix bug') to highest (3, 'Deploy'), because compareTo() returns a negative, zero, or positive result reflecting that intended ordering for every pair of tasks Collections.sort happens to compare during the sort.

examples.title: The Same Objects, Sorted Two Different Ways With Two Comparators
examples.explanation: Neither sort() call here touches Task's own compareTo() at all: both pass a Comparator instead, which List.sort() uses in place of the elements' natural ordering. Comparator.comparing(Task::getName) builds a Comparator from a method reference, comparing tasks by whatever getName() returns using String's own natural (alphabetical) order; the second sort uses Comparator.comparingInt(Task::getPriority).reversed() to sort by priority but flip the direction, so higher priority numbers come first instead of the ascending order Task's own compareTo() would produce. The same three Task objects get reordered completely differently by each call, with Task's source code never changing at all. This is the entire point of keeping ordering logic external to the class via Comparator, rather than being limited to whatever single order compareTo() happens to define.

examples.title: Multi-Key Sorting With thenComparing
examples.explanation: The primary key is grade, sorted in its natural (alphabetical) ascending order via Comparator.comparing, which groups Amy and Cara (both grade A) ahead of Ben (grade B). Within that A group, thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder()) only gets consulted as a tie-breaker for pairs whose grade comparison already returned zero (Amy and Cara) and it orders that specific subgroup by gpa in descending order, putting the higher GPA first: Cara (3.9) before Amy (3.8). Ben, having a different grade, is never compared against them by gpa at all; the grade comparison alone already placed him last, after both A-grade students. The final order is therefore Cara, then Amy, then Ben.

misconceptions.description: A class can implement Comparable multiple times, or in multiple ways, to support different orderings for different situations.
misconceptions.clarification: A class can implement Comparable<T> only once: it's a single method, compareTo(), and a class either has one natural ordering or none at all; there's no mechanism to define several different compareTo() overloads or variants for different contexts. When a class needs to be sorted in more than one way, the natural ordering (if any) belongs in compareTo(), and every other ordering is expressed as a separate Comparator object, defined wherever it's needed, independent of the class itself and of each other.
misconceptions.fact: A class can implement Comparable<T> once: it's a single method, compareTo(), and a class either has one natural ordering or none at all; there's no mechanism to define several different compareTo() overloads or variants for different contexts.

misconceptions.description: Since sorting just needs SOME consistent order, the exact numeric value returned by compareTo() (not just its sign) matters and gets used by sorting algorithms.
misconceptions.clarification: Only the sign of compareTo()'s return value is ever meaningful: negative, zero, or positive, never its magnitude. Returning -1 versus -1000000 for 'this comes before other' produces identical sorting behavior; no sorting algorithm or sorted collection in the standard library ever inspects or uses the numeric size of the returned value for anything. This matters practically because it means overly-clever-looking compareTo() implementations that try to encode 'how much bigger' one object is than another via the return value's magnitude are not doing anything sorting-relevant with that extra information, because every consumer of compareTo() discards it.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Collections.sort(players) with no second argument uses Player's compareTo(). Which field does it compare by, and in which direction?
The second sort call passes a Comparator built from p.name. It replaces compareTo() for that call and does not combine with it.
Comparator.comparing((Player p) -> p.name) compares the extracted names using String's natural (alphabetical) order.
exercises.expectedAnswer: [Kim:50, Lee:65, Jo:80] then [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65]. The first sort uses compareTo(), ascending by score. The second uses a Comparator by name, which replaces the score-based order with alphabetical order.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Collections.sort(players) with no Comparator falls back to each element's own compareTo(), which Player defines to compare by score ascending, so the first printed list orders Kim(50), Lee(65), Jo(80) from lowest to highest score. The second sort call passes Comparator.comparing((Player p) -> p.name), which replaces the ordering used for this call: it does not defer to or combine with compareTo() in any way. That Comparator extracts each Player's name and compares using String's natural alphabetical order, giving Jo, Kim, Lee alphabetically, so the second printed list is [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65], completely unrelated to the score-based order from the line before it.

exercises.prompt: This compareTo() implementation is meant to sort Products by price ascending, but sorting a large list of Products with extreme price values occasionally produces an incorrectly-ordered result. Find and fix the bug.
hints: this.priceInCents - other.priceInCents is ordinary int subtraction. What happens if the true difference between two extreme int values does not fit in an int?
int overflow wraps around in Java without an exception, which can flip the sign of the result.
Use the static Integer.compare(a, b) instead, which returns the correct sign without overflow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: this.priceInCents - other.priceInCents computes the mathematical difference using ordinary int arithmetic, which has a fixed range: if priceInCents holds values near Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE respectively (or close enough to those extremes), the true difference can exceed what an int can represent, and Java's int arithmetic wraps around (overflows) rather than throwing any error. That wraparound can flip the sign of the result, making compareTo() report 'this is smaller' when it's larger, or vice versa, which corrupts the sort for those extreme-value pairs while appearing to work correctly for every ordinary-sized value, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. Integer.compare(a, b) is implemented to avoid this: it returns the correct sign for any two int values without ever performing a subtraction that could overflow, which is why it (along with Double.compare, Long.compare, and the other wrapper-class compare() methods) is the idiomatic, safe choice inside any compareTo() or Comparator, rather than hand-rolled subtraction.

assessments.prompt: A Product class already implements Comparable<Product> to sort by price ascending. A specific report needs Products sorted by name instead, just for that one report. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Write a separate Comparator<Product> that compares by name.
This isn't possible in Java -- once a class implements Comparable, no other ordering can ever be used to sort it.
Add a second compareTo() method to Product that takes no arguments and compares by name.
Change Product's compareTo() to compare by name instead of price, since a class should only ever need one ordering at a time.
assessments.explanation: A Comparator is the tool for a one-off or context-specific ordering that shouldn't change the class's own natural order: writing Comparator.comparing(Product::getName) and passing it to sort() for that one report leaves Product's existing compareTo() (and every other piece of code relying on its price-based natural order) completely unaffected. The “Change Product's compareTo() to compare by name…” option would break every other place in the codebase that currently relies on Product's natural price ordering, just to satisfy one report's different need. The “Add a second compareTo() method to Product…” option describes something Java doesn't support: compareTo() cannot be overloaded with a no-argument version; Comparable<T> mandates one compareTo(T) signature. The “This isn't possible in Java -- once…” option is false: sort() and List.sort() both readily accept a Comparator that overrides the natural order for that specific call, which is the mechanism this scenario calls for.

assessments.prompt: Explain the structural difference between Comparable and Comparator -- not just what each one is used for, but why a class can only have one Comparable ordering while supporting unlimited Comparators, and when you'd reach for each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Comparable<T> is a capability a class bakes into itself, once: implementing it means writing a single method, compareTo(T other), that defines the one ordering the class's own author considers 'natural' for that type, and because it's one method with one required signature, a class can express only one Comparable ordering, never several. Comparator<T>, by contrast, is not a method on the class being ordered at all: it's a completely separate object, implementing its own single method, compare(T a, T b), that some other piece of code writes to express whatever ordering it happens to need at that moment. Because a Comparator lives outside the class it orders, nothing stops any number of different Comparators from existing for the same type simultaneously, each expressing a different ordering, defined by different pieces of code, for different purposes, with zero coordination required between them and zero changes needed to the class itself. This asymmetry maps onto when to reach for each: Comparable is the right choice when a type has one obvious, intrinsic ordering that essentially everyone using that type would expect by default (numbers ordering by magnitude, dates ordering chronologically) and baking that into the class itself means callers get correct default sorting for free, with no per-call setup. Comparator is the right choice for every other ordering need: sorting by a different field, sorting in reverse, sorting by a combination of fields with specific tie-breaking rules, or sorting a type that has no obvious natural order at all (or one whose source code you don't even have access to modify). In code, it's completely normal for a type to define one sensible Comparable natural order and still have several different Comparators defined elsewhere for specific contexts that need something else: the two mechanisms are complementary, not competing.

assessments.prompt: Comparator<Student> cmp = Comparator.comparing((Student s) -> s.grade).thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder()); Two students, X (grade "B", gpa 3.5) and Y (grade "A", gpa 2.0), are compared with cmp.compare(X, Y). What does this comparison actually decide on, and what is the result's sign?
options: It decides based on gpa first, since thenComparing was written second in the chain but is actually evaluated with higher priority than comparing.
It decides based on grade alone, since "B".compareTo("A") is already nonzero -- gpa is never even consulted for this particular pair.
It throws an exception, because the two students differ in both grade and gpa at the same time.
It returns zero, treating X and Y as equal, because the chain combines both criteria into a single averaged comparison.
assessments.explanation: thenComparing is a tie-breaker, consulted only when the comparison before it returns zero. Comparing X and Y by grade already gives a nonzero result ("B" sorts after "A", so compare(X, Y) is positive), and the chain returns it immediately without reaching the gpa comparison. The “It decides based on gpa first, since…” option reverses how the chain evaluates; earlier keys are checked first and take priority. The “It throws an exception, because the two…” option invents a failure mode chained Comparators don't have. The “It returns zero, treating X and Y…” option is wrong because Comparator chaining never averages or blends criteria: each key is checked in strict sequence, only falling through to the next on an exact tie.

assessments.prompt: class Item implements Comparable<Item> { String label; int priority; public int compareTo(Item other) { return Integer.compare(priority, other.priority); } } -- equals() and hashCode() are left as Object's defaults. Item a = new Item("apple", 1); Item b = new Item("banana", 1); TreeSet<Item> set = new TreeSet<>(); set.add(a); set.add(b); System.out.println(set.size()); What prints, and why?
options: 2, because a and b are clearly different objects with different labels, so both are kept regardless of what compareTo() returns.
This throws an exception, because compareTo() returning 0 for two objects that are not .equals() violates a rule the compiler enforces.
1, because TreeSet uses compareTo() as its sole notion of equality internally, and a.compareTo(b) returns 0 (same priority).
2, because leaving equals() and hashCode() as Object's defaults makes TreeSet fall back to comparing object identity instead of using compareTo() at all.
assessments.explanation: Unlike HashSet, which uses equals() and hashCode() to detect duplicates, TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo() (or a supplied Comparator) as their only test for "same element". a and b both have priority 1, so a.compareTo(b) is 0, and TreeSet treats b as already present and keeps only the first, even though the labels differ and they are not .equals(). The “2, because a and b are clearly…” option assumes TreeSet checks equals(), which it does not for this purpose. The “This throws an exception, because compareTo() returning…” option invents a compiler-enforced consistency rule between compareTo() and equals() that doesn't exist: it's a strongly recommended convention, not something Java checks or rejects. The “2, because leaving equals() and hashCode()…” option is wrong because TreeSet's behavior here is not conditional on what equals()/hashCode() happen to be; it always uses compareTo()/Comparator for its internal ordering and duplicate detection.
